title: Shaping Useful Noise: Energy Distributions Predict Visual Pretraining Quality
claim: Summary statistics can match across datasets whose full distributions differ; a distribution-level metric exposes the difference that the summary hides.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right, equality/inequality formula boxes between them
description: A toy 2-D feature-space sketch with two panels. On the left, Q_A is a single blue density blob with concentric contours, labelled 'one mode, low-energy support'. On the right, Q_B is two separate modes: a red high-energy blob and a blue low-energy blob. Both panels have the same dashed 2σ ellipse and the same centre dot, marking the shared FID mean and covariance. Callouts label the FID ellipse and the density contours. Between the panels, two rounded boxes read 'FID(P,Q_A) = FID(P,Q_B)' and 'ELD(P,Q_A) ≠ ELD(P,Q_B)'. A legend at the bottom maps blue to low-energy mass and red to high-energy mass, and P is the real images. A subtitle sits at the top. The eye goes first to the two blobs and then to the equations in the middle.
caption: ELD distinguishes synthetic pretraining datasets FID cannot. Self-supervised pretraining benefits when synthetic data spans the full likelihood spectrum of real images; sources with identical FID can carry very different energy distributions, which ELD detects.
abstract: Synthetic data can scale visual pretraining, but current selection criteria only partially explain which datasets train strong representations. We propose using the energy profile of a dataset--the distribution of log-probability levels it occupies under a normalised real-image density model--as an audit and curation principle for synthetic data. To operationalise this view, we introduce Energy-Level Distribution Distance (ELD), which compares real and synthetic energy distributions. Real images span sparse high-likelihood scenes and dense low-likelihood textures, so useful synthetic data should cover this energy range rather than collapse to likely but low-variation samples. Across diverse synthetic datasets, ELD exposes mismatches missed by FID and predicts pretraining performance beyond FID, LPIPS variation, and feature-space recall, including across CNN and ViT self-supervised settings. We then use ELD to resample and mix synthetic sources, matching the real-image energy histogram while preserving diversity and improving downstream transfer.
